paper_metadata.title: Antiepileptic drug withdrawal in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study used a systematic search of medical records in a defined geographic region (Buskerud county) covering 9.1% of the Norwegian population. The recruitment was consecutive and included home visits to minimize selection bias, achieving a 69% participation rate which is robust for this type of retrospective-to-interview design.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Drammen Hospital serves the inhabitants of Buskerud county and four neighboring municipalities, that is, a population of 477 000 people, or 9.1% of Norway's total population.
items.reasoning: The geographic and demographic context of the source population is clearly defined.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: Recruitment of patients was based on a search of medical records at Drammen Hospital in the time period 1999‐2013. All medical records containing an International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD‐10) code of epilepsy (G40) were reviewed.
items.reasoning: The study used a comprehensive ICD-10 search and explained the referral patterns (private neurologists/pediatricians referring to the hospital for EEG) to justify the sampling frame.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: The clinical interviews were conducted between November 2016 and February 2018
items.reasoning: The specific dates for the interview phase are provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Drammen Hospital, Norway... Buskerud county and four neighboring municipalities
items.reasoning: The setting is a regional hospital in Norway with specific geographic coverage.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: all patients with genetic generalized epilepsy (GGE) aged 14‐40 years were invited... Patients older than 40 years were not contacted... The definition of JME was based on the consensus on diagnosing and management of JME issued in 2013.
items.reasoning: Age limits and diagnostic consensus criteria are explicitly stated.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: We contacted 205 patients with GGE, of which 141 (69%) agreed to participate in the study.
items.reasoning: A 69% participation rate is acceptable for a study requiring clinical interviews and home visits.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Demographic and clinical characteristics of the patients with JME and other types of GGE are summarized in Table 1.
items.reasoning: Table 1 provides age, sex, epilepsy duration, and seizure types.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While the study identifies the proportion of the baseline sample available (69%), it does not provide a detailed comparison of characteristics between those who participated and those who declined (31%). This leaves some uncertainty regarding informative censoring.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: 141 (69%) agreed to participate in the study.
items.reasoning: 69% is good, but nearly one-third of the identified population is missing.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study does not describe attempts to characterize or follow up with the 64 patients who declined participation.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Reasons for non-participation (declining the interview) are not detailed.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No data is provided for the non-participants.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Without data on non-participants, it is impossible to determine if the analyzed sample is biased.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factors (age at onset, seizure types, EEG features) were measured using standardized clinical interviews and verified against medical records and EEG recordings, ensuring high reliability.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Variables potentially influencing AED self‐withdrawal were analyzed one by one, as were variables potentially influencing the outcome of withdrawal.
items.reasoning: Factors like age at first motor seizure, PPR in EEG, and psychosocial factors are clearly defined in Tables 2 and 3.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Patients were classified as JME or non‐JME based on information from the clinical interview, medical records, and EEG recordings.
items.reasoning: Triangulation of interview data with medical records and objective EEG data increases reliability.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Student's t tests were used for comparison of continuous variables
items.reasoning: Continuous variables like age and BIS/HADS scores were analyzed as such without arbitrary dichotomization.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: A semistructured questionnaire designed for the purpose of this study was used.
items.reasoning: All participants underwent the same interview protocol.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: Table 2 and 3
items.reasoning: The tables show N=87 for JME and N=35 for withdrawal, indicating complete data for the analyzed groups.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Imputation was not mentioned; however, missing data appears minimal.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The primary outcome (seizure freedom after withdrawal) relied on patient recall during a one-time interview. While medical records were used for verification, the retrospective nature and reliance on self-reporting for 'self-withdrawal' events introduce potential recall bias.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Twelve of those who discontinued AEDs (34%) were free from generalized tonic‐clonic seizures (GTCS) and without antiepileptic drugs >1 year.
items.reasoning: The outcome is clearly defined as GTCS freedom for >1 year off medication.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: The clinical interviews were conducted... independent of regular clinical follow‐up. This probably contributed to more reliable answers
items.reasoning: While independent interviews help, the outcome is still based on subjective recall of seizures.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: A semistructured questionnaire designed for the purpose of this study was used.
items.reasoning: Standardized interview for all participants.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study performed only univariable analyses (t-tests and chi-square). As noted by the authors, the sample size was too small for multivariable regression, meaning they could not adjust for potential confounders (e.g., adjusting the effect of 'age at onset' for 'seizure type').

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: Variables potentially influencing AED self‐withdrawal were analyzed one by one... (Table 2 and 3)
items.reasoning: The study measured age, duration, seizure types, and psychosocial factors.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Polytherapy was defined as two or more AEDs used concomitantly. Self‐withdrawal was defined as intentional discontinuation...
items.reasoning: Definitions for clinical and social variables are provided.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: HADS is scored on a 0‐42 point scale... Total BIS score may range from 30 to 120
items.reasoning: Validated scales (HADS, BIS) were used for psychological confounders.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: The clinical interviews were conducted between November 2016 and February 2018 at Drammen Hospital or in the participant's home.
items.reasoning: Consistent setting and tools for all.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No imputation used.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study did not use matching or stratification in the design.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Variables potentially influencing AED self‐withdrawal were analyzed one by one... Regression models would have been valuable... but restricted sample size [made them] less suitable.
items.reasoning: The authors explicitly state they did not perform multivariable adjustment.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The analysis is transparent about its limitations, but the use of multiple univariable tests without adjustment for multiple comparisons or confounding increases the risk of spurious findings. Reporting is otherwise comprehensive.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Student's t tests were used for comparison of continuous variables, and chi‐square tests were used for comparison of categorical variables
items.reasoning: The statistical plan is clearly laid out.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Variables potentially influencing AED self‐withdrawal were analyzed one by one
items.reasoning: No multivariable model was built; analysis was limited to bivariate associations.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: restricted sample size, making sophisticated statistical methods like logistic regression less suitable.
items.reasoning: While the authors justify the lack of regression due to sample size, univariable analysis is insufficient for prognostic modeling.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Tables 2 and 3
items.reasoning: The tables report on all variables mentioned in the methods, including non-significant results.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Statistical Analysis and Presentation Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: The statistical analysis is appropriate for the design of the study, limiting potential for presentation of invalid or spurious results.
